Sources of American Law
Objective:  Analyze the Process and Hierarchy of American Law

units.label: slide 2
units.text:
American Legal Heritage
There are four basic types of laws in the United States
Constitutional Law
Statute Law
Administrative Law
Case Law

units.label: slide 3
units.text:
Constitutional Law
Constitutional Law – Deals with the formation, construction, and interpretation of constitutions
Constitutional Law also decides the limits of government's power and the rights of individuals
Framework for the organization of the U.S. Governments
Since its inception in 1787, the Constitution has been amended  27 times
The first 10 Amendments are known as the Bill of Rights

units.label: slide 5
units.text:
Constitutional Law
More than any other relationship, constitutional law is thought to govern the relationship between an individual and the Federal government
Much of Constitutional Law deals with interpreting the constitution
How does it relate to the individual rights and freedoms of a citizen?

units.label: slide 6
units.text:
Statutory Law
Statutory Law – a statute is a law written by a legislative branch
Statutes may limit citizens' behavior or grant them rights and benefits
It may be on a Federal, State, or Local level
Statutes of lower jurisdictions are subordinate to the law of a higher jurisdiction
Federal > State > Local
Federal Law may not cover all areas, so it is up to the state to decide for itself

units.label: slide 7
units.text:
How Statutory Law is made


In the U.S. Laws start as a Bill
Bills are given a number and sent to Congress for a vote 
Before the vote is cast there is presentation, debate and often resolutions made
After is passes, Congress it is then sent to the House of Representatives for a second vote
Then goes to the President, who, signs it into law
Veto? → back for more debate (unless 2/3 majority)

units.label: slide 8
units.text:
Animal Example
At the federal level, statutes regarding animals usually focus on the interstate aspects of our relationships to animals
Protection of migratory birds, for example, or the importation, interstate transportation and sale of endangered animals are covered by federal statutes
States still have authority to regulate animals within their borders 
Bought and sold, protection, treatment, etc.

units.label: slide 10
units.text:
Administrative Law


Administrative Law – spells out the authority and procedures to be followed by government agencies
Is law regulating the powers, procedures, and acts of public administration
 It applies to all public officials and public agencies
Cannot make decisions outside of their jurisdiction

units.label: slide 11
units.text:
Case Law/Common Law
Case Law – the single most important basis of American Law
Case Law is a law made by judges in the process of resolving a case
When a judge hears a case that is similar to an earlier case, the judge follows the precedent
Reported decisions of appeals courts and other courts which make new interpretations of the law and, therefore, can be sited as precedents
American judges not only apply the law, they also make the law, to the extent their decisions in the cases before them become precedent for decisions in future cases
That’s why some laws are always changing

units.label: slide 12
units.text:
Equity and Principles 


Equity – is a system of rules by which disputes are resolved on the grounds of fairness
Four basic principals underline the operations of the American Legal System
Equal justice under the law – treat all people the same
Due Process of law
Substantive – laws themselves are fair and equal
Procedural – No arbitrary enforcement of law, laws must follow their own rules

units.label: slide 13
units.text:
Principles


Adversarial System - The court room acts as an arena in which lawyers from opposing sides present their best argument 
 Presumption of Innocence – All accused people are innocent until proven guilty
the burden of proof belongs to the prosecution or accuser
